title: In those days (Luke 2:1–7)
hook: an emperor counts his people, and God arrives uncounted

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Benedictus, Zechariah's song when his tongue was loosed. Your line was the dayspring from on high. Did you greet the light this morning before the phone? Day five hundred eight.

Somewhere in Rome, an order goes out. Count everyone, so the empire knows who it can tax. It's the kind of thing powerful people do without thinking twice: a line in a decree, and ordinary lives rearranged. Families pack up and go, each to their own city, to be registered. And among them, walking from Nazareth in Galilee to Bethlehem in Judea, are Joseph, of the house of David, and Mary, the young woman he's engaged to, who is great with child. The emperor will never hear their names. He's counting heads, not looking at faces.

Luke opens the scene like a history book, in the King James Bible: "And it came to pass in those days, that there went out a decree from Caesar Augustus, that all the world should be taxed." Caesar Augustus, emperor of Rome. Some readers puzzle over how this census fits other records of the time, and Luke doesn't stop to explain. He's more interested in the contrast. The emperor's decree moves Joseph and Mary to Bethlehem, David's town, little Bethlehem from Micah, without the emperor ever knowing. Then, in just two verses, the birth itself: "she brought forth her firstborn son, and wrapped him in swaddling clothes, and laid him in a manger; because there was no room for them in the inn." That's it. No angels yet, no star, no description of the night. A feeding trough for a crib. And notice what isn't there. There's no innkeeper in the story. Nobody slams a door. Luke's Greek word for inn is the same one he uses later for the guestchamber where Jesus eats the Passover with his friends. So some scholars picture a family house with its guest room already full, and the baby laid where the animals fed. Readers notice the shape of it. The emperor sits at the center of the world, counting. And in the Christian telling, God arrives at its edge, uncounted, in a crowded place, in a feeding trough. Some see a hint of the end of Luke's story, when his body is wrapped in linen and laid in a tomb hewn in stone.
screen: `THE CENTER COUNTS; GOD COMES TO THE EDGE.`
then, large: `THERE WAS NO ROOM FOR THEM IN THE INN.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: notice the small in the big news. Settle, and breathe. Think of today's headlines, or whatever's been dominating your feed: an election, a market, a war, a celebrity, a policy. Big names, big numbers. Now look underneath. Who are the people at the edges of that story, the ones who'll never be named? A family packing up. A nurse on a night shift. A child somewhere in the crowd. Pick one and hold them in mind for a moment, by face, not by number. If you pray, you can pray for them. If you don't, simply let them matter to you for a minute. The bell holds the time.
In those days. The opening of Luke's birth story: an emperor counts the world, and Jesus is born at its edge, laid in a manger.
Your line: not counted, but there. Today, when you read the news, look for one person the headline missed, and keep them in mind until evening. Day five hundred eight.

howItsDone: Luke 2:1–20 is a Christmas reading in churches, and some families read it aloud at home on Christmas Eve or at the Christmas table.

myth: Luke's story has an innkeeper who turns them away
no innkeeper appears. the text says only there was no room for them in the inn, perhaps a guest room.
Luke describes the birth itself in very few words
two verses: she brought forth her son, wrapped him and laid him in a manger.
Luke's word for inn is used again for the room of the Last Supper
the same Greek word, kataluma, names the guest chamber in Luke 22.

fork.setup: you're Joseph, in Bethlehem with Mary about to give birth, and the guest room is full. where is the baby laid?
options: in a manger, a feeding trough.
fork.reveal: she "laid him in a manger; because there was no room for them in the inn." a feeding trough for a crib.

original.note: Greek: a lodging, a guest room. usually translated inn in Luke 2:7, and guestchamber in Luke 22:11.

trapdoor: what you thought: a cruel innkeeper shut the door on Mary.
what it means: an emperor counts the world for taxes, and Jesus is born at its edge, in a crowded house, laid in a feeding trough.
what a scholar hears: kataluma, Luke's word for inn, is also his word for the guestchamber of the Last Supper, so some read the house as full, not hostile.

sources.quoted: And it came to pass in those days, that there went out a decree from Caesar Augustus, that all the world should be taxed.

notes: The census under Quirinius (Luke 2:2) and its dating relative to Herod's death is a known historical problem; the script says only that historians debate how it fits the records.
Augustus hailed as savior and bringer of peace in inscriptions (e.g. the Priene calendar inscription). Confirm.

Kataluma as guest room (Luke 22:11 'guestchamber') and the reading of a full family house with animals inside: a widely held scholarly view (e.g. Kenneth Bailey), not universal. Presented as 'many scholars think'.
The tomb hint (Luke 23:53; Joseph of Arimathea's tomb) is offered as what 'some see'.
Day 490 (Micah 5:2) referenced as 'little Bethlehem from Micah'.

Editor review (2026-10-01): SERIOUS fixes: Joseph was called 'a carpenter' (Luke never says so; Matthew 13:55) and the tomb 'belonged to someone else' (that is Matthew 27:60; Luke 23:53 says only a new tomb hewn in stone), so the tomb echo now uses Luke's own 'wrapped ... laid'. Also cut the unsourced 'marble office', 'millions of lives', 'most powerful man on earth', the Priene-style 'inscriptions hailed him savior' line and 'historians still debate' (now 'some readers puzzle'); kataluma framed as what some scholars picture, not 'many scholars think'; 'God arrives' attributed to the Christian telling; howItsDone softened.
